coach_says: Your extra pawn on e5 is guarded by the bishop on c3, and Black's knight on e4 is attacking that bishop. After castling, Black simply plays Nxc3 and then wins e5 back with the knight on c6 and Bg4 hitting your f3 knight. Instead take the knight first with Bxe4: after dxe4 the pawn on e4 is loose and you collect it (Qxe4, or Rd1 hitting the queen first), going two pawns up. When an enemy piece attacks the guard of something important, ask whether you can remove that piece before you make a quiet move.
also: win a second pawn with Bxe4

coach_says: Your bishop on c4 was attacked by the knight on d6, and you are a pawn down after Nxe4. Ng5 goes after f7, but f7 is well defended and Black just takes your bishop with Nxc4, then h6 kicks the knight back. Bb3 keeps the bishop, and then Re1 and Nxe5 win your pawn back. Deal with the piece that is attacked first, and attack only when the attack actually threatens something.

White's bishop on d5 attacks your rook on a8, but it is standing right in front of White's queen on the d-file. Rd8! attacks it and uses that: if Bxa8, Rxd1+ wins the queen for a rook, so White has to spend a move saving the bishop while your rook takes the open file. Bb7 just blocks and swaps off your good bishop, letting White castle in comfort. When a piece attacks you, look for a counterattack that hits it, especially when it is lined up with something bigger behind it.
also: piece lined up with the queen

coach_says: Nh6+ puts your two knights side by side on the edge, on g6 and h6, and the white king can step to h5 and attack both at once. A check with the g6 knight leaves the h6 one hanging, and retreating it allows Rd4+, which hits your king and your bishop on e4 because the f6 bishop guards d4. Ne5+ keeps the knights central and working together. Before you check, ask where the king will go and what it will attack there.

Your bishop on a7 is out of play after grabbing that pawn, and Black's rooks own the d-file. Qc7 attacks b7 and d8, but R2d7 defends and hits your queen, so it has to go back and you have spent two moves for nothing. Bd4 brings the bishop back to the centre, blocks the d-file and eyes the f6 knight. When your opponent is pressing, bring stray pieces back before going on a raid with the queen.

With ...b5 and ...a6 already played, d4 walks into a known trap: after Nxd4 Nxd4 exd4 Qxd4, Black plays c5 hitting your queen and then c4 hitting your bishop on b3. The bishop has to hide on a2, where it is buried behind the b5 and c4 pawns, and your e4 pawn becomes weak. Quietly playing d3 or Ba2 first avoids it. When your bishop sits on b3 against pawns on a6 and b5, watch for ...c5 and ...c4 coming with tempo.

f6 does nothing for your development: it takes the best square from your g8 knight and opens the diagonal from c4 to g8 and the one from h5 to e8 towards your king. After d4 and Bc4 you will struggle to castle kingside. Develop a piece instead, like Nf6, Bf5 or c6, and only move the pawns in front of your king for a concrete reason.

Both captures win the f7 pawn back, but take it with the rook. Rxf7 puts a rook on the seventh rank, where it eats g7 next, and with Black's king and kingside pieces still at home, Bg5+ adds more threats. After Bxf7 the bishop is simply hit by Ke7 and has to move again. When you can recapture with a rook that lands on the seventh rank, that is usually the stronger choice.

Bxa2 grabs a pawn, but after b3 your bishop is shut in on a2 and needs time to escape, while Re2 pins your knight on e5 to your king. You were already better with active pieces. Bd7 keeps the bishop in play and lets your knight jump to g4 to press White. Before grabbing an edge pawn with a bishop, check whether a pawn move can cut off its way back.

Qb3+ only sends the black king to g7, where it is safer than on f7, and your queen then has to come back. You are two pawns down after Bxf7+, so every move must do something. b4 attacks the c5 bishop, gains space and makes room for Nc4 to swap off that strong bishop. A check is only good if the king ends up worse off or you gain something from it.
also: gain time on the c5 bishop

coach_says: g6 leaves holes on the dark squares f6 and h6, and it lets Bg5 come in, pinning your e7 knight to your queen and heading for f6. Ng6 instead gets the knight off e7 to an active square and frees your bishop, and you can castle quickly. In the opening, prefer developing moves to pawn moves in front of your king.

The f3 pawn was attacked twice, by your queen and the h5 bishop, and defended only once by White's queen. Qxf3 Qxf3 Bxf3 wins a clean pawn and swaps queens when you are already ahead. Qg6 lets Rg1 chase your queen off the sixth rank, and then the d6 pawn falls to Nxd6. Count attackers and defenders on every pawn your pieces are hitting.

Both white knights, on d5 and g4, are aiming at f6, and your king is still in the centre. After Nb4, White plays Ndxf6+ gxf6 Nxf6+ and your king is stripped bare and can no longer castle. Nxd5 removes one of the attackers first and the danger is gone. Before starting your own play, ask what your opponent is threatening, especially sacrifices next to your king.

Bh5+ sends the king to d8, which is fine for Black, and then ...g5 and ...Nf6 hit your bishop so it has to go back to f3: two moves wasted. Black's real threat was g5 against your f4 bishop. Bg3 or Na3 deals with that and gets on with development. Don't give a check just because you can; ask what it gains.

Black's knights on g6 and h6 are side by side and both g5 and h5 let your king attack them. On g5, though, the h6 knight escapes with Nf7+, so you never get time to take the other. On h5, a check from the g6 knight leaves h6 hanging, and if the h6 knight retreats, Rd4+ forks the king and the e4 bishop since your f6 bishop guards d4. When forking with the king, pick the square where the targets can't escape with check.
also: rook check forks king and bishop

coach_says: Good move: Bxg7 wins a pawn and the h8 rook will follow. You are winning heavily either way, just keep picking up the loose pieces.
Ne4 is the best move here: it hits the queen on f6 and the d6 bishop, gaining time and heading to swap off Black's good bishop. Well played.
You are well ahead in material, and g6 keeps it that way. Qf6 was a little sharper, using the queen with checks on c3, but either move keeps a winning position.
Kg2 is fine: the knight on h2 is short of squares and your king heads for the kingside, where your g7 pawn will decide the game. Kg3 or Kf2 would be just as good.
Your position was already very difficult, and Qf6 is about as good as anything else here. Moving the queen off the e-file so Rxe5 is no longer possible was the right priority.
